newsitem.title: UK: Experts see UK election poll as rogue result.
newsitem.headline: Experts see UK election poll as rogue result.

text.p: The polling organisation which set the British election battle alight on Wednesday, with a dramatic narrowing of the gap between the two major parties, stood by a result which flies in the face of findings from most other forecasters.

ICM spokesman Nick Sparrow said he was happy with the conduct of and the findings from the poll in Wednesday's Guardian newspaper, which put the opposition Labour party just five points ahead of the ruling Conservatives.
"There is no perfect way to conduct a poll, it is a choice between imperfect alternatives," Sparrow told Reuters.
"But if there had been any doubt at all about this poll, I would not have allowed the findings to be published," he said.
Poll experts said that at first sight, ICM had come up with a rogue poll, something which is expected to happen about once in every 20 surveys.

"I think the best judgment is that it is a rogue poll, although there may be an indication that the Labour lead is narrowing a little bit," said political scientist John Curtice of the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow.

Curtice pointed out that ICM had conducted a poll in Scotland in recent days which showed the Conservatives losing ground. "You would have expected to find some evidence in the Scottish poll of the change we see in today's national poll. But it wasn't there," he said.

John Benyon, political scientist at the University of Leicester, agreed that ICM's was probably a rogue result. "This always seems to happen at least once in every election campaign. We reckon that one in every 20 polls is a rogue," he said.

The ICM/Guardian poll, which has consistently predicted a narrower margin between the two main parties than most other newspaper surveys, put Labour on 42 percent, with the Conservatives on 37 percent.
This compares with ICM's poll for the Guardian last week, which gave Labour a 14-point lead on 45 percent.
According to the poll, the Conservatives have made up a lot of ground at the expense of the third-placed Liberal Democrats, which slipped to 14 percent from last week's 19 percent.

It is the first time the Labour party's lead in any national opinion poll has fallen to single figures since November 1993, and bolsters the fading fortunes of the Conservative party as the British election campaign nears its final week.

ICM's research is at odds with the findings from most other polls -- in Wednesday's Daily Telegraph a poll by Gallup put the Labour lead 21 points ahead of the Conservatives on 51 percent. This is five points higher than Tuesday's findings from its "rolling poll", which reports every 24 hours.

And the latest findings from a Reuters panel of Britain's top polling experts, published on Wednesday, put the average Labour lead at nine points, with 44 percent of the vote compared with the Conservatives' 35 percent.
This, according to the average findings of the Reuters panel, would give Labour an 82-seat majority in parliament, up slightly on the forecast of a 79 seat majority a week ago.
